articles.title: Income Redistribution: Problems of Politics and Migration
articles.abstract: Why does sub-national political polarization in the United States produce redistributive inefficiency, and how can migratory externalities compound those inefficiencies? This paper uses public choice theory to argue that political reform is inseparable from redistributive solutions.

articles.title: Changes in Japan's Labor and Immigration Policy Address Depopulation Concerns
articles.abstract: This paper analyzes Japan's June 2024 expansion of its foreign worker visa program against the backdrop of decades of demographic decline, declining birth rates, and a shrinking labor supply. It surveys the policy responses considered over that period ("Womenomics," productivity reforms, the new visa legislation) and asks whether any combination of them can address a problem this ingrained in Japan's economy.

articles.title: A Recipe for Disaster: How Change, Money and Behavior Create Financial Crises
articles.abstract: Financial crises from the South Sea Bubble to the Crash of 1929 have a common set of prerequisites, namely: novel change, easy money, and irrational human behavior. This paper argues that all three must be present to produce a sustained market panic; no single factor is sufficient to cause collapse on its own.

articles.title: Will the Green Transition Save China's Economic Growth?
articles.abstract: Examines whether China's green energy sector can replace the infrastructure investment, real estate development, and credit expansion that drove GDP growth for decades. In 2023, renewable energy accounted for an estimated 40% of overall GDP growth, bringing up the question of whether this trajectory is sustainable as traditional drivers stagnate.

articles.title: L'état, C'est Quoi?: Balanced Power versus Absolute Rule in the Rupture of Financial Bubbles
articles.abstract: In response to the  South Sea and Mississippi Bubbles of the early 18th century, Britain's constitutional framework, with the Bank of England as lender of last resort, enabled recovery, while France's unchecked absolutist monarchy amplified the disaster and delayed financial development for generations. This article closes by considering the implications for checks on monetary authority today.
